01 — OVERVIEW

Recovering diversity after distillation

Timestep distillation makes diffusion models fast. But adversarial objectives can concentrate their outputs, trading away diversity. We recover much of that lost diversity by merging a distilled student with its full-step teacher.

Our framework decomposes their weight difference into low-rank directions, then learns how much of each direction to merge through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Quality and diversity guide the merge, using just one calibration prompt.

03 — METHOD

Low-rank policy-optimized merging

Optimize the merge in weight space,
rather than backpropagating through generation.

LOW-RANK WEIGHT SPACE

Instead of one global interpolation coefficient, assign a separate coefficient to each singular-vector pair. This makes merging more expressive while keeping its representation compact.

06 — ABSTRACT

Abstract

Diffusion models enable high-fidelity, diverse image synthesis but incur high deployment cost, motivating timestep distillation. To mitigate blurriness, distillation methods widely adopt adversarial objectives, which frequently reduce sample diversity. Existing merging methods can raise diversity, but only at the cost of quality. To recover diversity without this quality penalty, we propose a low-rank policy-optimized model merging framework that combines the teacher’s diversity with the student’s efficiency.

Specifically, we decompose the teacher–student weight difference matrices via low-rank decomposition and optimize the coefficients of the resulting singular vectors, allowing finer-grained and memory-efficient merging. However, the student’s iterative few-step inference makes direct backpropagation through sampling intractable. We address this by modeling the interpolation coefficient logits as a Gaussian distribution policy and optimizing them via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), using image quality and diversity as reward signals.

Notably, this formulation remains highly data-efficient, requiring only a single text prompt for optimization. In contrast to prior merging methods, our method recovers much of the diversity lost to distillation while maintaining or improving quality and preference, achieving the best quality-diversity balance among merging approaches at the same inference cost. We demonstrate this on both SDXL and SD3.5-L, which differ in architecture and training objective.
